passed.title: join_asof matches the previous key by default and needs both sides sorted on the key
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.join_asof` defaults to `strategy='backward'`. Each left row gets the last right row whose key is less than or equal to its own key, not the nearest one. Exact key matches are accepted because `allow_exact_matches=True`. Left rows that have no earlier right key get null, just as in a left join. Both frames must be sorted by the `on` key (and within each `by` group), so call `LazyFrame.sort` first. Pass `strategy='forward'` or `strategy='nearest'` explicitly when that is what you mean.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

left = pl.LazyFrame({"t": [1, 5, 10], "x": ["a", "b", "c"]}).sort("t")
right = pl.LazyFrame({"t": [2, 5, 8], "v": [20, 50, 80]}).sort("t")

# default: backward search, exact matches allowed
print(left.join_asof(right, on="t").collect())
# forward search gives different values
print(left.join_asof(right, on="t", strategy="forward").collect())
# exclude exact key matches
print(left.join_asof(right, on="t", allow_exact_matches=False).collect())

passed.title: join_where is an inner join that does not preserve row order
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.join_where` performs an inner join, so left rows that satisfy no predicate disappear. It is not a left join. A left row can also appear several times, once per matching right row. The row order of the inputs is not preserved, so sort the result with `LazyFrame.sort` if you need deterministic output. When a column name exists in both frames, refer to the right-hand column with its suffix (default `_right`) in the predicate. The API is experimental.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

east = pl.LazyFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "lo": [0, 10, 20]})
west = pl.LazyFrame({"wid": [7, 8], "val": [5, 15]})

out = (
    east.join_where(west, pl.col("val") > pl.col("lo"))
    .sort("id", "wid")
    .collect()
)
# id=3 is gone (no match); id=1 appears twice
print(out)
print(out.height)

passed.title: interpolate turns integer columns into Float64 and leaves edge nulls
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.interpolate` is linear, and integer columns come back as `f64`, as the docstring example shows. Code that expects the original integer dtype will break. Nulls at the start and end of a column are not filled; they stay null. Add `Expr.forward_fill` / `Expr.backward_fill` (or `Expr.fill_null`) for the edges. Cast back with `LazyFrame.cast` if you need integers.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [None, 1, None, 3, None]})

out = lf.interpolate().collect()
print(out)  # [null, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, null] as f64
print(out.dtypes)

fixed = (
    lf.interpolate()
    .with_columns(pl.col("a").forward_fill().backward_fill())
    .cast({"a": pl.Int64})
    .collect()
)
print(fixed)

passed.title: explode keeps empty and null lists as null rows by default
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.explode` defaults to `empty_as_null=True` and `keep_nulls=True`. An empty list becomes one row with a null value, and so does a null list. This differs from SQL-style `UNNEST`, which drops those rows. Counts and joins on the exploded frame then include phantom null rows. Pass `empty_as_null=False, keep_nulls=False` to drop them instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"k": ["a", "b", "c"], "v": [[1, 2], [], None]})

default = lf.explode("v").collect()
print(default)  # b and c each produce a null row
print(default.height)

dropped = lf.explode("v", empty_as_null=False, keep_nulls=False).collect()
print(dropped)
print(dropped.height)

passed.title: cast is strict by default, and strict=False silently produces nulls
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.cast` defaults to `strict=True`. A value that cannot be represented in the target type, such as an overflow, raises an error. On a LazyFrame that error surfaces only at `LazyFrame.collect`, not at the `cast` call. Setting `strict=False` does not clamp or wrap the value: it silently replaces it with null. Check `LazyFrame.null_count` afterwards if you rely on non-strict casts.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 300]})

plan = lf.cast({"a": pl.UInt8})  # no error yet: lazy
try:
    plan.collect()
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

loose = lf.cast({"a": pl.UInt8}, strict=False)
print(loose.collect())  # 300 became null
print(loose.null_count().collect())

passed.title: drop and rename raise on unknown columns unless strict=False
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.drop` and `LazyFrame.rename` default to `strict=True`. Naming a column that is not in the schema raises an error. Do not expect it to be ignored, and there is no pandas-style `errors='ignore'` argument. Pass `strict=False` to skip missing names. For `LazyFrame.rename`, `strict` has no effect when you pass a function as the mapping.

note.title: Resolve a LazyFrame schema once with collect_schema instead of .columns/.dtypes/.schema
note.trap: On a LazyFrame, `LazyFrame.columns`, `LazyFrame.dtypes` and `LazyFrame.schema` resolve the whole schema on every access. That can mean reading file metadata or making network requests for scanned sources. These properties exist only for symmetry with `DataFrame`. Call `LazyFrame.collect_schema` once, keep the result, and read names and dtypes from it, especially inside loops or comprehensions.
note.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"foo": [1, 2], "bar": [1.5, 2.5], "ham": ["a", "b"]})
lf = lf.with_columns((pl.col("foo") * 2).alias("foo2"))

schema = lf.collect_schema()  # resolve once
numeric = [name for name, dtype in schema.items() if dtype.is_numeric()]
print(numeric)
print(lf.select(numeric).collect())
